input: The pump affinity laws are a very useful set of relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its operating speed is changed. In essence, there are three simple proportionalities that together capture the behaviour of the pump. Firstly, the flow delivered by the pump varies in direct proportion to the speed, so that if the speed is doubled, the flow is doubled as well. Secondly, the head developed by the pump varies with the square of the speed, which means that the head responds much more strongly to a change in speed than the flow does. Thirdly, the power absorbed by the pump varies with the cube of the speed, making the power the most sensitive of the three quantities to any change in operating speed. These relationships can be illustrated with a simple worked check: doubling the speed multiplies the flow by 2, the head by 4 and the power by 8. This dramatic increase in power is one of the key reasons why speed is adjusted so carefully in practice, since a relatively modest increase in speed, and hence in flow, can lead to a disproportionately large increase in the power that has to be supplied. It is important to remember that the affinity laws are statements about ratios between two operating speeds of the same pump, rather than absolute predictions, and that they rest on the assumption that the efficiency of the pump does not change significantly between the two speeds in question. The laws are at their most reliable when they are applied over a moderate range of speeds around the point at which the performance of the pump is actually known.
target: The pump affinity laws relate the duty of a centrifugal pump at one speed to the duty of the same pump at another speed. Flow varies in direct proportion to speed: at twice the speed the pump delivers twice the flow, through the same impeller and against the same system. Head varies with the square of the speed, so the head responds more strongly to a speed change than the flow does. Power varies with the cube of the speed, and responds most strongly of the three quantities. Each law takes the same form: the quantity at the new speed is its value at the known speed, multiplied by the ratio of the speeds raised to the power the law assigns to that quantity. Flow counts as a volume rate, head as the energy the pump adds to each unit weight of liquid, and power as the shaft power the driver must supply at the duty point. A worked check fixes the pattern of the three laws together. Doubling the speed multiplies the flow by 2, the head by 4 and the power by 8. The check shows why speed is set with care: a rise in speed buys flow at the first power and pays for power at the third, so the power consequence of a speed change is settled before the speed is raised. The laws state ratios, not absolute duties. An absolute duty at a new speed is calculated from a measured or rated duty at a known speed, and no affinity law supplies the starting duty itself. The proportionalities presume the same pump, the same liquid and a system that is unchanged between the two speeds, with efficiency taken as unchanged as well; where efficiency shifts between speeds, the power proportion is the first of the three to depart from the stated ratio.
